items.title: Machine Learning and Large Language Models for Maternal Cardiometabolic Risk Prediction Across Harmonised Public Pregnancy Datasets
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Pregnancy-related cardiometabolic complications remain important contributors to adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. However, risk-prediction models developed from a single dataset often have limited transportability, and the role of large language models in maternal risk stratification remains unclear. Methods We used two publicly available datasets: the Maternal Health Risk dataset and the Preeclampsia in Pregnant Women dataset. Low-risk, mid-risk, and high-risk labels were harmonised, and a binary high-risk versus non-high-risk endpoint was constructed. We compared several machine-learning models and undertook internal cross-validation, external validation, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and sensitivity analyses. Structured records were subsequently converted into label-free case narratives; DeepSeek and Qwen were evaluated under different prompting strategies, and the concordance between keywords in large language model explanations and machine-learning feature importance was examined. Results In internal validation, HistGradientBoosting showed the strongest overall performance, with a macro-averaged F1 score of approximately 0.876. Performance declined in external validation, in which multiclass accuracy was approximately 0.389. Across sensitivity analyses, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.437 to 0.528. Among the large language model configurations, Qwen with few-shot chain-of-thought prompting performed best, with an accuracy of approximately 0.583 and a macro-averaged F1 score of approximately 0.467. Explanatory keywords generated by the large language models most often concerned blood glucose or diabetes, blood pressure or hypertension, haemoglobin or anaemia, previous complications or medical history, and proteinuria. Conclusion We developed an integrated framework for maternal cardiometabolic risk prediction that combines feature harmonisation, conventional machine learning, external validation, and large language model explanations. Machine-learning models performed well internally but generalised poorly across datasets. Large language models showed some ability to assess risk from case text and generate readable clinical explanations, but require validation in larger, multicentre, prospective studies.

items.title: Deep learning integrated clinical-radiomics model for prognostic prediction in locally advanced cervical cancer through 18 F-FDG PET/CT and MRI combination
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Precise pretreatment risk stratification is critical for guiding treatment intensification and personalized follow‑up in patients with locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) after concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). This study developed and validated a deep learning integrated clinical-radiomics model for prognosis prediction in patients with LACC treated with CCRT, using dual-modal pretreatment imaging from 18 F-FDG PET/CT and contrast-enhanced MRI. Methods We retrospectively collected 346 patients (276 for training and 70 for testing) with LACC between June 2016 and October 2021. Radiomics and deep learning signatures were extracted from PET/CT and MRI. These signatures were integrated with the clinicopathological factors into a nomogram for clinical applications. Models were constructed using eleven machine learning algorithms, and a clinical-radiomics-deep learning model (CRDLM) was developed. The evaluation of the model’s performance was conducted through the metrics of the area under the curve (AUC). Results The CRDLM demonstrated superior predictive performance (AUCs of 0.998 (95% CI: 1.00–1.00) for training cohort and 0.901 (95% CI: 0.83–0.97) for testing cohort), which is significantly superior to conventional clinical factors (FIGO stage and SCC-Ag, AUC = 0.605–0.658). In addition, the CRDLM which combined radiomics with deep learning significantly outperformed the radiomics‑only model (AUC = 0.793, p = 0.006). Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of CRDLM reached 0.947, 0.725, and 0.786, respectively. Conclusions The CRDLM provides robust prediction of disease progression in LACC patients who received CCRT, which may facilitate personalized treatment strategies and improve clinical outcomes. Further validation in multicenter prospective studies is warranted.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Liver Disease Prediction: A Systematic Review and an Explainable Hybrid Ensemble with Automated Clinical Feature Engineering
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Liver disease prediction using routine clinical biomarkers is a common medical artificial-intelligence problem, there are significant variations in reported performance on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) and these differences stem from variations in preprocessing, feature selection, class balancing, validation and leakage control. This study integrates a DOI verified systematic evidence review, a reproducible experimental benchmark and an explainable hybrid ensemble. Structured data studies published between 2020 and September 2026 that include a DOI were synthesized, especially for the current focus of the research on ILPD. All 583 ILPD records (of 416 liver-disease and 167 non-disease cases) were used in the experimental component. The data-quality analysis, followed by false-discovery-rate (FDR) corrected group testing, repeated stratified cross-validation and by duplicate-sensitivity analysis were followed by nested 5×3-fold model development. Four complementary learners extra trees, LightGBM, Gaussian Naive Bayes and logistic regression were stacked with leakage safe out-of-fold stacking and sigmoid calibration. An automated clinical feature-engineering module expanded the 10 original predictors to a 24-feature candidate pool using clinically interpretable ratios, composite biomarkers, and log transformations; mutual-information feature selection was tuned strictly inside training folds. In the systematic review, DOI-verified studies reported headline accuracies ranging from approximately 71% to 99.6%, but evaluation protocols were highly heterogeneous. In our leakage-aware experiment, automated feature engineering improved ROC-AUC from 0.744 to 0.761 and PR-AUC from 0.893 to 0.897. Under a balanced-accuracy threshold, the engineered model achieved 64.8% accuracy, 71.2% balanced accuracy, 56.3% sensitivity, 86.2% specificity, and 0.761 ROC-AUC. Under a training-only sensitivity-constrained threshold, it achieved 69.5% accuracy, 78.1% sensitivity, 47.9% specificity, F1 = 0.785, and MCC = 0.258. Age, ALT, AST, indirect bilirubin, bilirubin burden, ALT + AST, and log-transformed bilirubin/aminotransferases were selected in every nested-CV model-fit. The findings show that automated clinical feature engineering improves discrimination and screening trade-offs, while also demonstrating that very high headline accuracy on small tabular medical datasets should be interpreted in the context of validation design and leakage control.

items.title: Re-evaluating the benefit of pretraining scale in cell foundation models
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell foundation models are self-supervised neural networks pretrained on millions of cellular transcriptomes to learn representations that transfer across biological domains and downstream tasks. Recent benchmarks have questioned the training data scaling law for these models, showing early finetuning performance saturation on a fraction of available pretraining data. However, whether this trend holds for larger second-generation foundation models, and whether it reflects genuine saturation of foundation representations remains unclear. To resolve these aspects, we tested the performance of second- and first-generation cell foundation models across corpus sizes using the standard finetuning approach, and extended it with a comprehensive fully frozen evaluation. We revealed that the training-data scaling relationship becomes apparent under fully frozen finetuning, particularly for second-generation models. Zero-shot analyses similarly recovered dependence on pretraining scale. We conclude that finetuning performance saturation does not imply biological representations saturation, and that a shift in standards of cell foundation model evaluation is needed, complementing standard finetuning with fully frozen benchmarking to capture the quality of the foundation representations.

items.title: Generative steering to adapt proteins beyond native biological contexts
items.abstract_or_text: Proteins evolved for native biological contexts often fail when deployed in new cellular environments or therapeutic settings. We present ProVADA, a test-time framework that steers a pretrained protein generator toward externally defined properties while preserving functional constraints. Its Mixture-Adaptation Directed Annealing sampler combines coordinated mutations, population selection, and annealing to navigate rugged objective landscapes. Experimentally, ProVADA converted secreted human renin into an active, drug-inhibitable cytosolic protease and extensively deimmunized two murine single-chain antibody fragments to reduce HLA visibility while retaining antigen recognition. ESCAPE-seq measurements confirmed substantial depletion of HLA-I binder peptides across alleles. Deimmunized FMC63 variants retained CAR-T-cell killing and showed fewer binders than a tested humanized comparator. Together, these results demonstrate that broad sequence redesign can adapt functional proteins to non-native biological contexts.

items.title: Large Language Models in Hearing Care
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) may support hearing care, but evidence of clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a scoping review across eight databases, with searches updated in September 2026. Among 110 included reports, 95 empirical analysis units comprised 62 model-centered benchmarks, 31 application-oriented investigations, and two adoption surveys. Applications addressed assessment scoring, clinical documentation, rehabilitation content, biomedical evidence processing, psychosocial support, and research. Fourteen empirical units evaluated prototypes or target users; none tested prospective service deployment or comparative clinical impact. Privacy evaluation concerned attitudes or perceived confidentiality; no included study tested technical privacy safeguards. Current evidence supports selected task-specific capabilities, not established improvements in care. Future research should prioritize applications addressing defined hearing-care needs and compare them with usual care or simpler alternatives. Evaluation should measure patient and professional benefit, safety, privacy, accessibility, and workload rather than response accuracy alone.

items.title: Functional fine-mapping of the 9p21.3 cardiovascular disease locus implicates the lncRNA MIR31HG as an effector transcript in endothelial cells
items.abstract_or_text: BACKGROUND: The chromosome 9p21.3 locus is among the strongest genetic risk loci for cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. Previous vascular disease studies focused predominantly on the role of this locus in smooth muscle cell (SMC) dysfunction, whereas its potential role in endothelial cells (ECs) remains less well characterized. Here, we sought to identify candidate regulatory variants at 9p21.3, their distal target genes, and effector transcripts that contribute to CVD-related phenotypes in ECs. METHODS: Promoter capture Hi-C was used to map chromatin interactions at 9p21.3 in primary human ascending aortic SMCs (n=6), supplementing the previously obtained ECs (n=16) dataset. To support the regulatory relevance of these interactions, expression quantitative trait locus analysis was performed in 136 vascular biopsies. Variant effects were prioritized in silico using AlphaGenome. The regulatory activity of the prioritized region was validated using CRISPR activation. RESULTS: Chromatin interaction mapping identified a complex regulatory architecture at the 9p21.3 locus involving 19 putative regulatory elements and 15 genes across ECs and SMCs. MIR31HG showed the most recurrent distal promoter connectivity with the 9p21.3 region. Consistent with the chromatin interaction map, expression of MIR31HG transcripts was associated with genetic variation at the 9p21.3 locus. In ECs, the lncRNA MIR31HG, but not miR-31, was responsive to hemodynamic flow. Depletion of MIR31HG in ECs was associated with endothelial activation. Epigenetic tracks and deep learning predictions highlighted an active enhancer element at 9p21.3, which was subsequently validated by CRISPR activation and increased MIR31HG expression, confirming its capacity to regulate MIR31HG over a large genomic distance of approximately 538 kb. CONCLUSIONS: Altogether, these data implicate lncRNA MIR31HG as a likely effector of the 9p21.3 CVD locus, linking the cis-regulatory element and heritable genetic variation in the respective region to endothelial activation through long-range enhancer regulation.

items.title: DeepD enables efficient genome modeling and controllable long-context sequence generation across domains of life
items.abstract_or_text: Genome foundation models hold great potential for advancing biological research, but modeling diverse complex genomes and generating controllable genome-scale sequences remain challenging. We present DeepD, a phylogeny-informed sparse mixture-of-experts model operating at single-nucleotide resolution over a 1-million-token context while reducing active computation. Pretrained on unselected whole-genome sequences across all domains of life, DeepD learns genic and intergenic sequence features and supports broad sequence-to-function prediction across species. DeepD performs well in human protein fitness and disease variants effect prediction, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2, with particular strength in regulatory regions, such as promoter and transcription-factor binding sites. Expert routing captures exon-intron boundaries, transposable elements, and distal cis-regulatory elements. DeepD also generates experimentally validated core promoters with specified transcriptional strengths. Finally, the Context-Anchor-Body strategy enables generation of complete yeast chromosome sequences and megabase-scale Arabidopsis segments, preserving gene structure and order while introducing variations within natural ranges. Together, DeepD is an efficient genome foundation model that unifies accurate sequence-to-function prediction with controllable genome-scale generation, advancing predictive and generative design of complex genomes.

items.title: Antibody-drug conjugate combination therapy targeting LGR5 and MET with different payloads enhances efficacy in preclinical colorectal cancer models
items.abstract_or_text: Leucine-rich repeat-containing G protein-coupled receptor 5 (LGR5) is a marker of cancer stem-like cells frequently upregulated in colorectal cancer (CRC) with lower expression in normal tissues, making it a favorable target for antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). ADCs combine antibody specificity with potent cytotoxic payloads to enhance efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity. LGR5-targeting ADCs incorporating different payloads demonstrate strong initial tumor inhibition, yet tumors eventually recur due in part to LGR5 downregulation, necessitating more effective strategies to prevent relapse. We show treatment with chemotherapies or an LGR5-targeting ADC coupled to a topoisomerase 1 inhibitor payload (8E11-CPT2) reduces LGR5 levels and increases MET receptor expression and/or activation in CRC cells, supporting a therapeutic approach to target LGR5 and MET simultaneously. Accordingly, we engineered a MET-targeting ADC (ABT-700-SG3199) via site-specific conjugation of the anti-MET antibody telisotuzumab (ABT-700) with the DNA-crosslinking pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimer SG3199. ABT-700-SG3199 exhibited superior potency and efficacy in CRC models compared to the clinical-stage MET-targeting ADCs ABBV-399 and ABBV-400, which use the same antibody backbone conjugated to different payloads. Treatment with ABT-700-SG3199 increased LGR5 expression, and the combination of ABT-700-SG3199 with 8E11-CPT2 enhanced CRC cell-killing efficacy, reinforcing the rationale for a dual-targeting approach. In patient-derived xenografts, combined administration of 8E11-CPT2 and ABT-700-SG3199 markedly delayed tumor relapse and prolonged survival compared with single-agent treatment. Taken together, these findings reveal a reciprocal regulation between MET and LGR5 in response to LGR5- or MET-targeting ADCs in CRC models and support a LGR5/MET dual-targeting therapeutic strategy to enhance efficacy and potentially overcome resistance and relapse.

items.title: Evidence-Grounded Large Language Model Reasoning for Patient Safety Using Knowledge Graphs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Development and Evaluation Study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Large language models have shown substantial potential for supporting clinical reasoning, but their use in patient safety applications remains constrained by limited access to structured clinical knowledge, variable evidence grounding, and difficulty tracing generated reasoning to supporting sources. Knowledge graphs can provide structured representations of clinical and safety concepts, while retrieval-augmented generation can incorporate relevant biomedical evidence into model inputs. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated framework for evidence-grounded patient safety reasoning that combines a large language model, a patient-safety knowledge graph, and retrieval-augmented generation. The study examined how structured knowledge and evidence retrieval contribute to concept extraction and reasoning performance. Methods The framework was developed using adult intensive care data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III and MIMIC-IV. Patient safety concepts were normalized using established clinical terminology and patient safety classifications and represented within a structured knowledge graph. An LLaMA-based language model adapted using low-rank adaptation was used for concept extraction and reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation incorporated relevant biomedical literature, patient safety resources, clinical guidelines, and drug-related knowledge using biomedical sentence embeddings and a FAISS-based vector index. Retrieved evidence was ranked using cosine similarity and incorporated into the model context together with relevant graph information. Performance was evaluated using F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and area under the precision-recall curve. Component ablation analyses examined the effects of removing the knowledge graph, low-rank adaptation, and retrieval augmentation.
